title: Theory of Partial Differential Equations
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L PDE curriculum: classification of second-order PDEs, first-order PDEs and the method of characteristics, the classical wave, heat and Laplace equations, and separation of variables/Fourier series solution methods.

questions.question: A partial differential equation (PDE) differs from an ordinary differential equation (ODE) in that a PDE:
options: Involves partial derivatives with respect to two or more independent variables
questions.correct_answer: Involves partial derivatives with respect to two or more independent variables
questions.explanation: PDEs involve functions of several independent variables and their partial derivatives, unlike ODEs which involve a single independent variable.

questions.question: The order of a PDE is determined by:
options: The highest-order partial derivative appearing in the equation
The number of terms in the equation
The degree of the dependent variable
questions.correct_answer: The highest-order partial derivative appearing in the equation
questions.explanation: Just as with ODEs, the order of a PDE is defined by its highest derivative, regardless of how many variables are involved.

questions.question: A general second-order linear PDE in two variables Auxx + Buxy + Cuyy + ... = 0 is classified as elliptic when:
questions.explanation: This discriminant condition mirrors the classification of conics; a negative discriminant classifies the PDE as elliptic (e.g. Laplace's equation).

questions.question: A second-order linear PDE is classified as parabolic when its discriminant B^2 - 4AC equals:
questions.explanation: A vanishing discriminant classifies the PDE as parabolic, the type exhibited by the heat/diffusion equation.

questions.question: A second-order linear PDE is classified as hyperbolic when its discriminant B^2 - 4AC is:
questions.explanation: A positive discriminant classifies the PDE as hyperbolic, the type exhibited by the classical wave equation.

questions.question: The one-dimensional heat (diffusion) equation is written as:
questions.explanation: The heat equation is a parabolic PDE relating the first time derivative to the second spatial derivative, with k the thermal diffusivity.

questions.question: The one-dimensional wave equation for a vibrating string is written as:
questions.explanation: The classical wave equation relates the second time derivative to the second spatial derivative, with c the wave propagation speed.

questions.question: Laplace's equation in two dimensions is written as:
questions.explanation: Laplace's equation, the prototype elliptic PDE, requires the sum of the unmixed second partial derivatives (the Laplacian) to vanish.

questions.question: A function satisfying Laplace's equation is called:
questions.explanation: By definition, harmonic functions are precisely the solutions to Laplace's equation.

questions.question: A first-order linear PDE of the form P(x,y) ∂u/∂x + Q(x,y) ∂u/∂y = R(x,y) can be solved using:
questions.explanation: Lagrange's method reduces the first-order linear PDE to solving the auxiliary system dx/P = dy/Q = du/R along characteristic curves.

questions.question: In Lagrange's method, the auxiliary equations for Pux + Quy = R are:
options: P dx = Q dy = R du^{-1}
questions.explanation: This system of ordinary differential equations defines the characteristic curves along which the PDE reduces to simpler relations.

questions.question: Characteristic curves of a PDE are significant because:
options: Along them, the PDE reduces to an ordinary differential equation, and information/discontinuities propagate along them
They are always straight lines regardless of the PDE
They only exist for elliptic PDEs
They represent points where no solution exists
questions.correct_answer: Along them, the PDE reduces to an ordinary differential equation, and information/discontinuities propagate along them
questions.explanation: Characteristics are curves along which the PDE simplifies, and for hyperbolic PDEs, they carry the propagation of wave-like disturbances.

questions.question: D'Alembert's solution to the wave equation utt = c²uxx with initial conditions u(x,0)=f(x), ut(x,0)=g(x) is given by:
questions.explanation: This closed-form solution to the 1D wave equation on the infinite line uses the general solution as a superposition of forward and backward traveling waves.

questions.question: The general solution of the 1D wave equation utt = c²uxx (without initial/boundary conditions applied) can be written as:
options: u(x,t) = F(x+ct) + G(x-ct), for arbitrary functions F and G
questions.correct_answer: u(x,t) = F(x+ct) + G(x-ct), for arbitrary functions F and G
questions.explanation: This is d'Alembert's general solution, representing the superposition of two waves traveling in opposite directions at speed c.

questions.question: The method of separation of variables assumes a solution of the PDE can be written as:
options: A product of functions, each depending on only one of the independent variables, e.g. u(x,t) = X(x)T(t)
A sum of the independent variables
A single function of all variables combined into one
questions.correct_answer: A product of functions, each depending on only one of the independent variables, e.g. u(x,t) = X(x)T(t)
questions.explanation: This product ansatz allows the PDE to be split into separate ODEs for each factor, each depending on only one variable, connected via a separation constant.

questions.question: When separating variables for the heat equation ut = k uxx with u = X(x)T(t), the resulting equations typically take the form:
questions.explanation: Since the left side depends only on x and the right only on t, both must equal a constant (-λ), splitting the PDE into two ODEs.

questions.question: In solving boundary value problems via separation of variables, the values of the separation constant λ for which nontrivial solutions exist are called:
questions.explanation: The boundary conditions restrict λ to a discrete set of eigenvalues, each associated with an eigenfunction solving the spatial ODE.

questions.question: After separation of variables, the final solution to a PDE with given boundary conditions is typically expressed as:
options: An infinite series (Fourier series) summing the product solutions weighted by coefficients determined from initial conditions
The average of the boundary values
questions.correct_answer: An infinite series (Fourier series) summing the product solutions weighted by coefficients determined from initial conditions
questions.explanation: Because the PDE is linear, a superposition (Fourier series) of the eigenfunction solutions is used to match arbitrary initial/boundary data.

questions.question: For the heat equation on [0,L] with u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0, the spatial eigenfunctions are typically:
questions.explanation: Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions (zero at both ends) select sine eigenfunctions that vanish at x=0 and x=L.

questions.question: Boundary conditions that specify the value of the solution u itself on the boundary are called:
questions.explanation: Dirichlet conditions prescribe the function's value directly on the boundary, as opposed to Neumann conditions which prescribe the normal derivative.

questions.question: Boundary conditions that specify the normal derivative (e.g. ∂u/∂n) on the boundary are called:
questions.explanation: Neumann conditions prescribe the derivative of the solution (e.g. flux) rather than its value, common in heat-flow problems with insulated boundaries.

questions.question: A Robin (mixed) boundary condition is a linear combination of:
options: The function value and its normal derivative on the boundary
questions.correct_answer: The function value and its normal derivative on the boundary
questions.explanation: Robin conditions combine both Dirichlet-type and Neumann-type information, as in modeling convective heat exchange at a boundary.

questions.question: A well-posed PDE problem (in the Hadamard sense) requires that a solution:
options: Exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the given data
Is always expressible in closed form
questions.correct_answer: Exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the given data
questions.explanation: Hadamard's well-posedness criteria (existence, uniqueness, stability/continuous dependence) are central to the theory of PDEs.

questions.question: The principle of superposition for linear homogeneous PDEs states that:
options: If u1 and u2 are solutions, then any linear combination c1u1 + c2u2 is also a solution
It applies only to nonlinear PDEs
questions.correct_answer: If u1 and u2 are solutions, then any linear combination c1u1 + c2u2 is also a solution
questions.explanation: Linearity of the PDE and its homogeneous boundary conditions guarantees that linear combinations of solutions remain solutions.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a quasi-linear PDE (linear in its highest-order derivatives but not necessarily in lower-order terms)?
options: u ∂u/∂x + ∂u/∂y = 0 (a form of the inviscid Burgers' equation)
questions.correct_answer: u ∂u/∂x + ∂u/∂y = 0 (a form of the inviscid Burgers' equation)
questions.explanation: This equation is linear in the highest derivatives (∂u/∂x, ∂u/∂y) but the coefficient u itself is the unknown function, making it quasi-linear rather than fully linear.

questions.question: The two-dimensional Laplace equation in polar coordinates (r,θ) is written as:
questions.explanation: Transforming the Cartesian Laplacian into polar coordinates introduces the extra first-derivative and curvature terms shown here.

questions.question: Poisson's equation differs from Laplace's equation in that:
options: It has a nonzero right-hand side (source) term: ∇²u = f(x,y)
It cannot be solved by separation of variables
questions.correct_answer: It has a nonzero right-hand side (source) term: ∇²u = f(x,y)
questions.explanation: Poisson's equation generalizes Laplace's equation by allowing a nonzero forcing/source function f on the right-hand side.

questions.question: The maximum principle for harmonic functions states that:
options: A harmonic function on a bounded domain attains its maximum (and minimum) value on the boundary of the domain
A harmonic function always attains its maximum at the centre of the domain
Harmonic functions have no maximum or minimum
The maximum value is always zero
questions.correct_answer: A harmonic function on a bounded domain attains its maximum (and minimum) value on the boundary of the domain
questions.explanation: This important property of solutions to Laplace's equation follows from the mean value property of harmonic functions.

questions.question: In the heat equation, the parabolic classification reflects the physical fact that:
options: Heat diffuses instantaneously (in the idealized model) and irreversibly, smoothing out initial temperature variations over time
Heat propagates as a wave with finite speed and no dissipation
There is no time dependence in heat conduction
Temperature oscillates periodically forever without damping
questions.correct_answer: Heat diffuses instantaneously (in the idealized model) and irreversibly, smoothing out initial temperature variations over time
questions.explanation: Parabolic PDEs like the heat equation model diffusive, irreversible smoothing processes, distinct from the reversible, finite-speed propagation of hyperbolic wave equations.
